title: Feedback-Enhanced Quantum Metrology and Clock Precision under Thermodynamic Uncertainty
abstract: Feedback can convert continuously monitored quantum jumps into a thermodynamic resource. We formulate full counting statistics for open quantum systems under unital jump feedback by incorporating the feedback maps into the tilted generator. The resulting trajectory ensemble determines both current fluctuations and the Fisher information of the measurement record. We show that feedback can enhance reservoir-parameter estimation and clock precision without necessarily changing average thermodynamic currents. This enhanced precision is not bounded by reservoir entropy production alone. By embedding the reduced dynamics in an enlarged measurement-feedback process, we derive a feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation in which the information entropy production of the feedback apparatus supplies the missing cost. A charge-monitored double quantum dot illustrates the framework: jump-conditioned feedback improves thermometry and chemical-potential sensing, and stabilizes a quantum clock defined by output-current ticks.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework showing that continuous quantum measurement and feedback can boost quantum sensing and clock accuracy in open systems. It derives a modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation proving that the achievable precision is limited not just by thermal dissipation, but also by the information cost associated with the feedback control itself.
main_problem: The paper investigates how continuous quantum measurement and feedback control can enhance quantum metrology and clock precision in open quantum systems, particularly concerning the limits imposed by thermodynamics.
main_result: Feedback enhances parameter estimation and clock precision beyond bounds set by reservoir entropy production alone, necessitating the inclusion of an information entropy cost from the feedback apparatus in the modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation.
method: The analysis employs full counting statistics derived from the tilted generator of the feedback-modified master equation, relating precision to the Fisher information and thermodynamic bounds to effective entropy production.
model_or_system: The framework is applied to open quantum systems, exemplified by a charge-monitored double quantum dot (DQD) coupled to thermal reservoirs, and generalized to a driven three-level system.
key_observables: Fisher information ($F_{fb}$), clock precision ($P_{clk}$), reservoir entropy production ($\dot{\Sigma}_{th}$), and information entropy production ($\dot{\Sigma}_{info}^{fb}$).
important_parameters: Feedback unitary angle ($\phi$), temperature ($T$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and detuning ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes unital jump feedback maps and relies on deriving the effective thermodynamic uncertainty relation by incorporating the information cost of the feedback process.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the enhancement of Fisher information and clock precision using feedback compared to no-feedback cases, and critically show that the reservoir-only TUR ratio falls below unity while the feedback-modified ratio remains above unity.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using full counting statistics and the tilted generator for feedback-modified dynamics. It then applies this to parameter estimation (DQD) and clock stabilization, culminating in the derivation and validation of the feedback-modified Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation using both electronic transport and general driven systems.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative link between measurement back-action, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and fundamental limits on precision, extending the standard fluctuation theorems to include active control mechanisms.

An open quantum system (center) exchanges energy and/or particles with a thermal reservoir, generating stochas- tic quantum jumps. A monitor continuously detects each jump and records its type and occurrence time. Conditioned on the detected jump type, a feedback controller immediately applies a unital operation Fk to the system. The monitor and controller together form the feedback loop.

FIG. 2. Feedback-enhanced thermometry with a charge- monitored DQD. (a) Schematic of the setup. The DQD is coupled to two electronic reservoirs at temperatures TL, TR and chemical potentials µL, µR. A left-injection jump LL,+ is continuously monitored. Conditioned on its detection, a fast unitary feedback pulse Uϕ rotates the post-jump state from the left dot toward the right dot, reshaping the subsequent waiting-time and jump statistics. The resulting feedback- controlled jump record is used to estimate TL.
